text: Hold every hour in your grasp. Lay hold of to-day's task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow's. While we are postponing, life speeds by. Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time. We were entrusted by nature with the ownership of this single fleeting and slippery possession, from which anyone who desires can cast us out. What fools these mortals be! They allow the cheapest and most useless things, which can easily be replaced, to be charged in the reckoning, after they have acquired them; but they never regard themselves as in debt when they have received some of that precious commodity, time! And yet time is the one loan which even a grateful recipient cannot repay.

If you would not have a man fear anything, let him consider that all things are to be feared. Strip off the mask from things, and look at the bare reality. Why do you fear death? It is the same as that which went before you; just as we felt no pain before our birth, so shall we feel none after our death. Do you think it is a great matter that you are living? All your slaves live, and all animals live. But it is a great matter to die honourably, prudently, bravely. Think how long you have been doing the same things: food, sleep, lust—this is the cycle. Not only a wise man, or a brave man, or an unhappy man, but even a fastidious man may wish to die, simply because he is tired of doing the same thing over and over.

Do you ask why such flight does not help you? It is because you flee along with yourself. You must lay aside the burdens of the mind; until you do this, no place will satisfy you. As Socrates said to one who made the same complaint: 'Why do you wonder that globetrotting does not help you, seeing that you always take yourself with you? The reason which drove you away is still at your heels.' What pleasure can there be in seeing new lands or visiting distant cities? All your restlessness is in vain. For you travel with your ailments; you follow yourself. You must change your soul, not your climate.

'They are slaves,' people say. Nay, rather they are men. 'They are slaves.' Nay, rather they are comrades. 'They are slaves.' Nay, rather they are humble friends. 'They are slaves.' Nay, rather they are our fellow-slaves, if one reflects that Fortune has equal power over them and over us. He whom you call your slave sprang from the same stock, is smiled upon by the same skies, and on equal terms with yourself breathes, lives, and dies. Treat your inferior as you would be treated by your superior. Remember that he whom you call your slave can look up at you and see in you a master who is equally a slave to fear, ambition, or desire.

chapter: Letter 63: On Grief for Lost Friends
text: Let not your eyes be dry when you have lost a friend, nor let them overflow. We may weep, but we must not wail. Do you think that you are likely to recover your friend by your tears? Any of us can find a friend, if we are worthy of friendship; and he who cannot make friends has no right to grieve over those he has lost. Let us see to it that the memory of our dead friends shall be a joy rather than a sorrow. It is natural to feel a pang when memory recalls them; but that pang is accompanied by a quiet pleasure. Let us greedily enjoy our friends, because we do not know how long this privilege will be ours. Death takes them away, but memory restores them to the mind.

chapter: Letter 78: On Healing and Bearing Pain
text: Pain is slight if opinion has added nothing to it; but if you take to encouraging yourself and say, 'It is nothing, or at least it is very slight; let us hold out, it will soon cease,' you will make it slight while you think it so. Everything depends on opinion; ambition, luxury, greed, harness themselves to opinion. It is according to opinion that we suffer. A man is as wretched as he has convinced himself he is. What does it matter how much pain one feels, if to bear it is a noble deed? Rouse yourself to resist: pain will cease or it will cease you; and in either case the torment is brought to an end.

The wise man is self-sufficient. He can do without friends, not that he desires to do without them, but that he can. When I say 'he can', I mean this: he bears the loss of a friend with equanimity. But he will never be without a friend, for he has it in his power how soon to replace him. Just as Phidias, if he lose a statue, can immediately carve another, so the master of the art of making friends will fill the vacant place at once. Why then do we seek friends? Not for personal advantage or to have someone sit by our sickbed, but to have someone whose sickbed we may sit by, someone whom we may rescue from the enemy.
